articles.title: Boatbuilders review – a gentle study of craftsmen’s quiet expertise
articles.summary: Venice film festival: Luke Lorentzen’s light-touch documentary follows a team of Maine craftsmen constructing a high-spec sailboat for a super-rich guy who seems kind of nice.
body: The Brooklin Boat Yard stands in a quiet harbour on the coast of Maine and makes high-spec yachts for rich men and women to sail. Its latest client is Graham Green, a millionaire financier who has commissioned the team to build him a 56ft cruising sailboat, the Kiandra, complete with maple worktops and a Sonos sound system. Green plans to sail the boat around the world, while its creators will stay in Brooklin, raise their kids and make boats. These men know their place. “We’re just the fucking help,” one confides.

Folded in amid the heat and hubbub of this year’s Venice film festival, Lorentzen’s serene piece of slow cinema provides both a cool palate cleanser and a paean to the pleasures of practical work. If you’ve ever watched Witness and wished that the barn-raising sequence was longer, then do seek this out: your cup will runneth over.
points: Venice film festival: Luke Lorentzen’s light-touch documentary follows a team of Maine craftsmen constructing a high-spec sailboat for a super-rich guy who seems kind of nice.

articles.title: Betty Gilpin Jabs at Sam Altman During ‘Manic Poem’ Acceptance Speech at the Emmys
articles.summary: “Widow’s Bay” guest star Betty Gilpin accepted her Emmy win for outstanding guest actress in a comedy by reading a poem she had written in jest — and very much in the unique style of the show. But it was one line that especially got the TV Academy audience at the Peacock Theatre to cheer:
body: “Thank you, Cosmo. My family, my daughters, friends — too many to name — my brothers Sam, Harry and my long dead dog Babe. Thank you.”
Where did the idea for the poem come from? Gilpin credited her episodic co-star Hamish Linklater, who also earned a guest actor in a comedy Emmy nomination for playing Richard Warren.

“I was on the same flight over as my co-nominee Hamish Linklater, and he came over to my row and was like, ‘Have you written a speech?’ And I was like, ‘Oh no, no, no! I’m not going to win,’” she said. “He’s like, ‘Well, you need to do that because it’s a scientific possibility, and don’t be stupid. Just prepare something.’ So he scared the shit out of me, and I wrote a quick manic poem, as you know, women have done for centuries. And I love my dog Babe. I named my first daughter after him. I’m almost ready for a dog, decade away.”
“Widow’s Bay” ended Night 2 of the 78th Emmys with eight wins — the most of any program so far. Gilpin called the recognition “incredible.”

articles.title: Film Industry Leaders Demand Structural Fix for Gender Gap at Lumiere Summit
articles.summary: Women held 17% of key behind-camera roles when the Celluloid Ceiling study began tracking the figure in 1998. Last year, that number stood at 23%. Six points in 27 years.
body: Berlinale festival director Tricia Tuttle cited her own festival’s data. In 2005, women directed 0% of films in Berlinale competition. By 2015 that had reached 15%, and by 2025 it stood at 40%. “Transparency makes you very aware, as a curator and as a decision-maker and a cultural gatekeeper, of what you’re doing,” Tuttle said. She added that data consistently shows films made with greater gender balance perform better commercially. “That’s a lot of creative energy that gets wasted,” Tuttle said, referring to the effort women are forced to spend justifying the conversation rather than making work.

articles.title: In the Shadows of Nuremberg review – trial-adjacent thriller aims to be Russian answer to Saving Private Ryan
articles.summary: A trivial personal plotline and a strain of maudlin patriotism undermine Nikolay Lebedev’s shaky telling of the Soviet side of the story. Taking place in the wings of the Nuremberg trial, this Soviet-side political thriller, first released back in 2023, features a scene in which the crowd turns on…
body: After his brother goes MIA in the vicinity of the soon-to-be-historic city, Red Army intelligence officer Igor Volgin (Sergey Kempo) wangles a post translating for the Soviet delegation. He’s approached by Lena (Lyubov Aksyonova), a Russian wastrel with a perfectly coiffed bob despite months of forced labour in a German munitions factory; she claims to have run into his sibling, an artist, in captivity. But she is also feeding information to Helmut (Wolfgang Cerny), a Nazi resistance diehard who believes Göring (Carsten Norgaard) and company should be accountable only to German courts.

articles.title: Imperium review – Sergei Loznitsa’s archive collage collates everyday life in cold-war Soviet Union
articles.summary: Venice film festival: The Two Prosecutors director cuts together documentary footage shot by a TV crew in the 1970s to try and get across what daily life in the USSR was like.
body: Here is an archive-compilation documentary from Sergei Loznitsa, a hypnotic panorama of early 1970s life across the vast reaches of the Soviet Union, or maybe we should call it the Soviet empire. Loznitsa gives it the Latin title Imperium, perhaps to recall the Romans before their decline and fall. His material is taken from fascinating footage shot between 1970 and 1973 by a visiting Italian camera crew who presumably had the necessary permissions and were well enough liked by the authorities to keep coming back.

What we do see is a demonstration of everyday life in the big cities of Moscow, Leningrad and Kyiv, with their shops and busy avenues, heartbreakingly provincial fashion shows and pop bands – but also the very un-modern rural traditions in various countries across Asia: traditions and norms that pre-existed the Soviet Union and carry on now, very possibly looking exactly the same in 2026 as they did in the early 70s. One weirdly pagan display appears to involve setting fire to an enormous phallus. Loznitsa introduces each segment with a resounding funeral bell with the screen cutting to a vivid and symbolic red.
points: Venice film festival: The Two Prosecutors director cuts together documentary footage shot by a TV crew in the 1970s to try and get across what daily life in the USSR was like.

articles.title: ‘Swiftly enchanted’: why Bedknobs and Broomsticks is my feelgood movie
articles.summary: The latest in our series of writers recommending their most rewatched comfort films is a reminder that Disney’s kids fantasy is more than a Mary Poppins knock-off. “ Filigree, apogee, pedigree, perigee!” – the four incantatory words I blame for receiving a shonky Paul Daniels Magic Set as a child…
body: When it became clear I wouldn’t deter the Third Reich with three plastic thimbles, a deck of playing cards and a flaccid wand, my conjuring kit was mothballed – but my irrational love of the Disney film remains to this day. For me, it originally fell into the category of the crackling VHS that your parents taped off ITV at Christmas then would repeatedly plonk you in front of to shut you up – to the point I can even recall the adverts.

But (non-Paul Daniels-branded) cards on the table: I’m a ’Knobs truther. As a working-class nipper, turning my bed into a DFS-based Tardis and hanging out with Jessica Fletcher-with-an-English-accent appealed more than a bossy nanny healing a posho family. Even now, I prefer its more offbeat, darker tone, and how its spoonfuls of sugar are strictly wartime-rationed.

articles.title: BBC News Anchor Maryam Moshiri Reveals Blood Cancer Diagnosis
articles.summary: BBC News anchor Maryam Moshiri has revealed she has been diagnosed with incurable blood cancer. The anchor, who joined the BBC in 2003, has covered events ranging from the Pope’s funeral to the Iran war since being diagnosed with Polycythaemia vera (PV) two years ago.
body: “It is going to be there till the day I die,” Moshiri said of her diagnosis. “A big part of this disease is having to get on with life.”

Among the treatments Moshiri has endured are twice-monthly venesections, where doctors remove blood through a vein, which she said was exhausting and left her feeling “extremely unwell.” Despite that, she travelled to Rome for two weeks last year to cover the death of Pope Francis.
On her return she underwent an immunotherapy treatment which resulted in “horrendous” side effects. She eventually switched to a different drug.

Moshri, who also has three children, decided to go public with her diagnosis in order to back a campaign by charity Blood Cancer U.K. called “Here for This,” which highlights the time sufferers miss with loved ones due to their treatment. She is also determined to continue working.

articles.title: Ellen Burstyn Cries as She Gets Venice Golden Lion for Lifetime Achievement: ‘It’s One Thing to Win an Oscar, Tony or Emmy — All of Which I’ve Won. But This Is a Lot’
articles.summary: Maggie Gyllenhaal delivered a message on behalf of Ellen Burstyn before the 93-year-old acting legend took the stage at the Venice Film Festival to receive the prestigious Golden Lion for Lifetime Achievement.
body: “You’re making me cry!” she said, which did little to stop the enthusiastic applause. “You’re overwhelming me, you know! I don’t know how to recover from that generous greeting.”
Burstyn has achieved a lot in her seven-decade career in Hollywood, which she was quick to remind the crowd, but she puts the Venice award among the top honors.
“You can’t imagine how meaningful this is to me It’s one thing to win an Oscar, a Tony or an Emmy — all of which I’ve won,” she said. “But this … it’s a lot.”
Since she learned she’d receive the Golden Lion, she said, she’s been reflecting on her life — and what it means to get a career tribute.

articles.title: Oasis: Don't Look Back In Anger review - emotional documentary glosses over the hard stuff
articles.summary: The film captures the euphoria of Oasis' comeback, but fails to explore the story of their reunion.
body: "The little things that used to annoy us about each other have all gone away," says Noel Gallagher of reconciling with his brother, Liam.

The scene comes towards the end of Don't Look Back In Anger, a sentimental and affectionate portrait of the band's comeback tour in 2025. But it's about as deep as we get into the band's 15-year hiatus.

In an opening montage, we hear how Oasis conquered the world in the 1990s with hits like Wonderwall and Roll With It. As their fame grew, so did the brothers' animosity, until the party came to an abrupt halt backstage at a gig in Paris in 2009.
Fan shot footage shows the promoter on stage, informing the crowd that the concert is cancelled following "a huge fight together in the dressing room".
points: The film captures the euphoria of Oasis' comeback, but fails to explore the story of their reunion.

articles.title: Jorja Smith, Chase & Status and Sam Smith to head up Radio 1's Live Lounge month
articles.summary: Jorja Smith, Rachel Chinouriri and Blossoms also among artists set to take to the studio next month.
body: Sam Smith, Chase & Status and Jorja Smith are among the artists who have been revealed for BBC Radio 1's Live Lounge month.
Indie band Blossoms, singer-songwriter Rachel Chinouriri and US rappers Anderson.Paak and Cordae will also take to the studio in October.
Each Live Lounge guest traditionally performs an acoustic version of one of their own songs, plus a cover of a track by a different artist.
The sessions will air on Radio 1's Live Lounge show, which will now be fronted by Charlie Hedges and Jeremiah Asiamah.

articles.title: ‘Alpha Gang’ Review: Cate Blanchett, Léa Seydoux and Dave Bautista Get Stranded in a Sci-Fi Comedy That’s All Flash and Zero Substance
articles.summary: Directed by David and Nathan Zellner ('Sasquatch Sunset'), the Telluride premiere follows aliens in '50s biker gear who've come to conquer Earth, but find newly human emotions get in the way.
body: Watching Alpha Gang, the new sci-fi comedy from Sasquatch Sunset filmmakers David and Nathan Zellner, it is very easy to imagine what a thrill it must have been to cook up the look of the thing.

It’s a striking hodgepodge of visual influences, and certainly an unusual one; I can’t think of another movie that climaxes with, essentially, medieval knights making their way through a Cold War nuclear bunker. But I also couldn’t quite tell you why this one does — or in fact why anything that happens in it happens at all. Premiering at Telluride, Alpha Gang is a mood board in search of a story.

It is at least possible to see that the script (written by both Zellners; only David is credited as director) intends to Say Something about what it means to be human in a time of great strife. The titular Alpha Gang are a star-studded sextet comprised of Léa Seydoux, Dave Bautista, Kelvin Harrison Jr., Lily-Rose Depp, Doona Bae and Riley Keough, their ID numbers (Alpha One, Alpha Two, etc.) going in that order. Like aliens from all over cinema, their mission here is to conquer, though they appear downright incurious about to what precise purpose.
